name: PRIDE
aliases: Program to Reduce Incontinence by Diet and Exercise
question: Does an intensive behavioral weight-loss program reduce urinary incontinence episodes more than structured education in overweight and obese women?

design.population: Women aged at least 30 years with BMI 25–50 kg/m² and at least 10 urinary-incontinence episodes in a 7-day diary.
design.locator: Subak 2009 full text, Methods: Participants, Study Design

verdictNote: The 6-month diary endpoint favored weight loss; pad-weight change did not differ between arms.
takeaway: In PRIDE, an intensive diet, activity, and behavior-change weight-loss program reduced weekly urinary-incontinence episodes more than structured education at 6 months (47% versus 28%) in overweight and obese women; the between-group reduction in stress episodes was also significant.

delivery.label: Weight-loss intervention
delivery.value: Weekly one-hour groups for 6 months, a 1,200–1,500-kcal/day diet, meal replacements, a goal of at least 200 minutes/week of activity, and behavioral skills training.

delivery.label: Education control and shared continence booklet
delivery.value: Four one-hour education sessions at months 1–4; both arms received a self-help bladder-control booklet at randomization.

results.measure: Pooled post-randomization association across weight-change categories
results.note: Compared with weight gain, 5% to <10% weight loss was associated with larger reductions in weekly urinary-incontinence episodes; no further improvement was detected at >=10% loss. Weight-change categories were not randomized.
